Well, I’m here because... for the past year or so, I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system is changing or, like, holding back parts of my dad’s lab results. 

I mean, I’m a phlebotomist, so I know exactly how the backend works. I draw blood all day over at the outpatient center. Mostly we use the lavender top tubes for CBCs, you know, the EDTA ones? We actually had a massive shortage of those last month, and my supervisor Brenda just completely botched the supply order. She’s always doing that, ordering the wrong gauge needles or forgetting the butterfly needles, and it makes my job so much harder when I have patients with rolling veins. No, I don't think so. I mean, people disagree with me all the time, but that's just because people don't pay attention to details. The strongest evidence? Well, it's what I saw with my own eyes. I drew his blood myself. I saw the labels, I know what tests I ran, and the numbers in the system just do not match what I saw. He has this really annoying laugh, too—it’s like a snort and a wheeze at the same time. I ruined a brand new pair of Dansko clogs stepping in it last Tuesday. They were the patent leather ones with the little blue flowers, too. Nobody's trying to hurt me or follow me around or anything like that. I mean, my life really isn't that interesting for anyone to want to monitor me. No, it’s definitely not an ordinary mistake. I mean, I’m here because for the past year I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system is deliberately changing or holding back parts of my dad’s lab results. It’s not just a typo.

I tell them to apply pressure, but they never do it long enough. They just slap the cotton ball on and let go. So yeah, I have to be energetic to get through a shift like that, but not... not unusually high or anything. Just normal busy. I just want to figure out this thing with my dad's chart, that's what's really keeping me up.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever heard voices or seen things that other people could not?\n\nPatient: No, definitely not. I don't hear voices or anything like that. I mean, the only thing I hear all day is the centrifuge humming. That machine is so old, it makes this awful high-pitched squeal whenever it's even slightly off-balance. And it's always off-balance because half the girls in the back don't know how to use a counterbalance tube. It's basic physics! You just put a water tube with the exact same volume directly across from the blood sample. But no, they just toss them in and hit start, and the whole machine starts vibrating across the counter. \n\nI told Sarah, our clinic manager—I said, \"Sarah, this thing is going to walk right off the edge one of these days and shatter a dozen samples.\" And she just nods and writes it on her little clipboard. She never goes anywhere without that clipboard, but I swear she just doodles on it because nothing ever actually gets fixed. Like the AC in the breakroom, that's been broken since July. We have this tiny little desk fan that just blows hot air around. It's miserable when you're wearing scrubs and a fluid-resistant lab coat all day. You just sit there sweating into your sandwich. \n\nSo... no, I don't hear or see things that aren't there. My hearing is perfectly fine. I just want people to actually listen to me when I tell them the truth about my dad's files.\n\nDoctor: Outside of your dad’s lab results, have you ever had another fixed belief that others strongly disagreed with?\n\nPatient: No, I don't think so. I mean, people disagree with me all the time, but that's just because people don't pay attention to details. Like my sister, she thinks I'm being ridiculous about Dad's chart, but she's the same person who thought you could put a wool sweater in the dryer on high heat. Seriously, she ruined this beautiful cable-knit sweater I got her for Christmas two years ago. Shrunk it down so small it would probably fit a toddler. And she tried to blame the washing machine! I told her, \"Amanda, it literally says 'lay flat to dry' on the tag.\" It's right there in plain English. \n\nBut nobody reads tags anymore. It's just like the labels on the biohazard bins at work. They have this huge sticker that says \"SHARPS ONLY,\" and yet, every single week, I find bloody gauze or empty alcohol prep pads shoved in there. It drives me absolutely insane. Do you know how expensive it is for the disposal company to take away the sharps containers? They charge by weight! And people are just filling them up with trash that could go in the regular red bags. I brought it up at the staff meeting last month, and they all just looked at me like I was being petty. But it's not petty, it's about following protocols. If you don't follow the rules for the little things, how can anyone trust you with the big things? Like lab results. \n\nSo, no, I don't have any other beliefs like that. I just notice things other people ignore.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever find this belief intrusive or unwanted, even if part of you wonders it might not be true?\n\nPatient: No, it's not unwanted because it's the truth. I don't wonder if it's not true. Why would I? I'm the one who drew his blood, I saw the labels, I know what I saw. It's not like I'm making this up for fun. Who would want to deal with this stress? \n\nHonestly, the real stress is just trying to get through a shift without losing my mind over the label printer. That thing is a nightmare. It jams every time you try to print more than five labels at once. And it's not a normal paper jam, either. The adhesive from the back of the labels melts onto the roller, so you have to sit there with an alcohol swab, scraping it off while the patient is just sitting in the chair staring at you. I told IT about it three weeks ago. Three weeks! And you know what they said? \"Have you tried turning it off and on again?\" I swear, I wanted to scream. I'm standing there with a biohazard tube in one hand, trying to keep a sterile field, and they want me to reboot a printer that's clearly got melted glue all over the internal mechanism. It's just like how nobody listens about the charts. You tell them exactly what the problem is, and they just give you some generic answer to make you go away.\n\nDoctor: Has this belief caused any major problems in your work, relationships, or daily life?\n\nPatient: Well, I mean... I guess people are acting a little weird about it. Like my family, they’ve actually started leaving me out of some of the appointment planning for him. Amanda took him to the clinic on Tuesday and didn't even text me until they were already driving home. Which is just... it's so irresponsible because Amanda doesn't even know what questions to ask the doctor. She probably just sat in the exam room playing on her phone. She just got that new one with the massive screen, and she is obsessed with this stupid gem-matching game. She was playing it at dinner last week! We went to Olive Garden for my mom's birthday and she just had it sitting right there next to her plate, tapping away. And the food was terrible, by the way. The breadsticks were completely cold. I don't know what's happening to restaurants lately, but you used to get steaming hot breadsticks, and now they just taste like cardboard that’s been sitting under a heat lamp for three hours. \n\nBut anyway, yeah, they leave me out of the medical stuff now. And at work... it's incredibly frustrating. I really feel like I’m no longer being considered for the lab supervision position. I overheard that people think I make record issues \"too confrontational.\" Confrontational! Just because I expect the charts to actually match reality. \n\nIt’s exactly like what happened with the supply closet last month. We kept running out of 21-gauge butterfly needles because the morning shift girls were hoarding them in their pockets. I literally saw Jessica stuffing a whole handful into her scrub pants. She wears those cargo scrubs with the huge side pockets. I tried a pair of those once, but the material is so stiff and they make your hips look ridiculously wide, so I just stick to the regular drawstring kind. They're much more breathable anyway. But I tried to bring up the needle inventory issue at the huddle, and suddenly *I'm* the bad guy for being too aggressive about it. So yeah, I guess wanting things documented and done right is causing problems, but only because nobody else wants to do their job properly.\n\nDoctor: What is the strongest evidence you have that your dad’s lab results were changed?\n\nPatient: The strongest evidence? Well, it's what I saw with my own eyes. I drew his blood myself. I saw the labels, I know what tests I ran, and the numbers in the system just do not match what I saw. For the past year, I've been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system is changing or holding back parts of his lab results. And no matter how many doctors or family members tell me the numbers are fine, I know the chart doesn't match what I saw. It's just... it's wearing me down. \n\nIt’s exhausting, honestly. Kind of like trying to find decent parking at the clinic. Have you ever tried parking in the east lot after 8:00 AM? It’s a complete nightmare. They have these three spots reserved for \"Employee of the Month,\" which is ridiculous because nobody even knows how you win Employee of the Month. I think it’s just a popularity contest. Last month, they gave it to Todd from Radiology, and all he does is stand by the vending machines talking about his fantasy football team. He has this really annoying laugh, too—it’s like a snort and a wheeze at the same time. Anyway, you have to park all the way out by the old dumpsters if you get there at 8:05, and when it rains, there’s this massive puddle that takes up two whole spaces. I ruined a brand new pair of Dansko clogs stepping in it last Tuesday. They were the patent leather ones with the little blue flowers, too. I tried wiping them down with a Clorox wipe, but the water had already soaked into the stitching. \n\nBut yeah, the evidence is that I know what I saw when I did the draw. I just know it.\n\nDoctor: Besides your dad’s lab results, have you ever felt that anyone was trying to harm, monitor, or control you?\n\nPatient: No, not at all. Nobody's trying to hurt me or follow me around or anything like that. I mean, my life really isn't that interesting for anyone to want to monitor me. Mostly I just go to work, come home, and watch TV. \n\nThough lately, I've been getting really into those home organization shows. Have you seen the one where they take everything out of the pantry and put it into those clear acrylic bins? It looks so satisfying, but honestly, who has the money for that? Those bins are like twenty dollars each at The Container Store. I went there last weekend just to look, and the prices are outrageous. And the store layout is so confusing. I got stuck in the custom closet section for like ten minutes because they had all these display walls set up like a maze. There was this lady in there with a tape measure, arguing with her husband about whether they needed the shoe rack or the pull-out hamper. He looked completely miserable. He was holding a half-empty iced coffee and just staring at the ceiling. I felt kind of bad for him, but also, if you're going to spend three thousand dollars on shelves, you should probably figure out where the shoes are going to go before you get to the store. \n\nBut anyway, no, I don't feel like anyone is out to get me or anything. Just the stuff with my dad's chart, that's the only thing that's wrong.\n\nDoctor: Have you been able to keep up with your daily routine and work normally over this past year?\n\nPatient: Yeah, I mean, outside of the whole dispute about my dad’s records, everything else is totally normal. I still go to all my phlebotomy shifts, I pay my bills on time, I take care of myself. I manage all my normal day-to-day responsibilities just fine. \n\nSpeaking of paying bills, though, the postal service has been driving me absolutely crazy lately. Our regular mail carrier, Gary, retired last month. He was great—he always made sure the letters were actually pushed all the way into the box so they wouldn't get wet. But this new guy, I don't even know his name, he just sort of jams them in there half-way. Last week, my electric bill got completely soaked because it rained and the envelope was just hanging out of the slot. And it's not like you can just dry it out, because the ink they use on those bills smears everywhere. I had to call the electric company to get my account number because I couldn't read the barcode, and I was on hold for forty-five minutes. They have this terrible hold music, too. It’s like a weird jazz flute playing the same five notes on a loop. I ended up putting it on speakerphone and folding laundry while I waited. I finally got this new detergent that smells like lavender and cedar, which is so much better than the chemical-smelling one I used to buy. It was on sale at Target, too. \n\nBut yeah, I keep up with everything. Work, home, all of it is fine. It’s just the stuff with the clinic that's the issue.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe your dad has been replaced by an identical-looking impostor?\n\nPatient: What? No. No, of course not. He's my dad. He's exactly the same person he's always been. He still tells those awful dad jokes, he still watches the History Channel at maximum volume... no, he hasn't been replaced by an impostor or anything crazy like that. \n\nThough, speaking of the History Channel, I really don't understand why they call it that anymore. Have you noticed? It's all just shows about aliens and pawn shops now. Last night, my dad was watching this marathon of that show where they dig for treasure on some island in Canada, and they never actually find anything. They just keep digging holes and finding, like, old nails and pieces of wood, and then the narrator makes it sound like it's the biggest discovery of the century. \"Could this rusty hinge belong to Marie Antoinette's lost jewelry box?\" No! It's a hinge! From a barn! But my dad will sit there for three hours just completely glued to it, eating those little pretzel sticks. He buys the pretzels in these massive plastic barrels from Costco. They get stale before you can even finish a quarter of them, but he refuses to buy the normal-sized bags because the barrel is a \"better value.\" I tried putting them in Ziploc bags to keep them fresh, but he said I was ruining his system. \n\nBut no, to answer your question, he's definitely my dad. Nothing like that.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a time when your mood was unusually high or irritable at the same time as this belief about your dad’s lab results?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't had anything like that. I'm not, like, bouncing off the walls or getting super irritable or anything. I mean, I get annoyed sometimes, but just normal annoyed. \n\nLike the other day in the breakroom at the clinic, they put up this incredibly passive-aggressive sign on the refrigerator about labeling your food. But the problem isn't the labels, it's that people leave their Tupperware in there until it literally grows mold. Last Tuesday I went to put my yogurt in there—just a plain Greek yogurt, I've been trying to eat healthier, maybe add some blueberries—and someone had left a half-eaten container of tuna salad right on the middle shelf. It smelled awful. Who brings tuna to a small clinic breakroom anyway? It's just so inconsiderate. And then the head nurse, Brenda, she started sending out these mass emails about \"refrigerator etiquette.\" She uses all caps and red font for the important words. It's like, Brenda, we're adults, we know how a fridge works, just throw the tuna away. I actually hit \"reply all\" by accident once when I was trying to forward one of her emails to my coworker, and I almost died of embarrassment. Luckily I caught it before I actually typed anything, but my heart was pounding. \n\nBut anyway, what were you asking? Oh, my mood. Yeah, no, my mood is totally normal. Just regular me. Nothing unusual going on there.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed your thoughts getting jumbled or hard for other people to follow?\n\nPatient: No, my thoughts are perfectly clear. People follow what I'm saying just fine. I mean, I talk to patients all day while I'm drawing their blood, and we have perfectly normal conversations. \n\nActually, I was talking to this one patient yesterday, Mr. Henderson. He comes in every two weeks to get his PT/INR checked because he's on blood thinners, and he was telling me about his garden. He grows these massive heirloom tomatoes, the ones that are kind of purple and green, you know? He brought me a picture on his phone, and they looked amazing. I tried growing tomatoes on my balcony last summer, but they just got these weird black spots on the bottom and died. I think I was watering them too much, or maybe not enough, I can never tell with plants. I bought this moisture meter thing from Home Depot that you're supposed to stick in the soil, but the needle just stayed in the middle no matter what I did. I ended up returning it. The line at customer service was ridiculous, though. There was this woman in front of me trying to return a ceiling fan that she had clearly already installed and taken down again, and she was arguing with the cashier about whether she had the original box. It was just a plain brown cardboard box, not even the one with the picture of the fan on it. \n\nBut no, nobody ever tells me my thoughts are jumbled or anything like that. I communicate perfectly fine.\n\nDoctor: Have you generally been suspicious that other people are untrustworthy or out to deceive you, even outside of your dad’s lab results?\n\nPatient: No, I'm not a suspicious person in general. I trust people just fine. I mean, most people are just trying to get through their day, right? \n\nLike the mailman. Our regular mailman, Greg, he's great. He always makes sure to put the packages all the way up on the porch so they don't get rained on. But last week, Greg was on vacation, and we had this substitute carrier. I don't know what his deal was, but he just left a package sitting right on the bottom step, completely exposed. And of course, it was raining that day. It was a pair of shoes I ordered online—just some comfortable slip-ons for work, because standing on your feet all day drawing blood really kills your arches. I used to wear those clogs that all the nurses wear, but they made my feet sweat too much. Anyway, the box was completely soaked through. I had to peel the cardboard off the shoes like wet papier-mâché. The shoes were fine, thankfully, they're kind of a waterproof material anyway, but it's just the principle of the thing, you know? If your job is to deliver mail, you should deliver it properly. I thought about calling the post office to complain, but then I figured, what's the point? You just wait on hold for twenty minutes listening to that terrible elevator music, and then whoever you talk to doesn't really care anyway. They just take down your information and throw it in a black hole. \n\nBut no, I don't walk around thinking everyone is out to get me or deceive me. I'm pretty trusting, honestly.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any other beliefs that others have told you are definitely untrue or impossible?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really had anything like that. People haven't told me my beliefs are impossible or anything. I mean, most people don't even know what I think about half the time, right? You just keep things to yourself. \n\nLike my neighbor, Mrs. Gable. She's always out in her yard, sweeping her driveway. Literally every day, sweeping away leaves that aren't even there. I don't tell her it's impossible to keep a driveway perfectly clean in the fall, I just wave and say good morning. She has this little dog, a Pomeranian mix or something, that just yaps at everything that walks by. Last week, it was barking at a squirrel for a solid twenty minutes. I was trying to watch this documentary on Netflix about competitive jigsaw puzzling—did you know that's a thing? People train for months to put together these thousand-piece puzzles in under two hours. They have special sorting trays and everything. I bought a puzzle once during the pandemic, one of those ones that's just a picture of baked beans. I thought it would be funny, but it was just infuriating. Every piece looked exactly the same. I left it on my dining table for three weeks before I finally just scooped it all back into the box. I think I lost a couple of pieces under the rug, though. My vacuum made this horrible crunching sound the next time I ran it. \n\nBut no, nobody tells me my beliefs are untrue. I just mind my own business, really.\n\nDoctor: Have there been any times when this belief about your dad’s lab results was present only when your mood was very depressed or very elevated?\n\nPatient: No, my mood doesn't really have anything to do with it. I mean, I'm just regular, you know? Sometimes I have a bad day at work, but that's normal. \n\nLike yesterday, we were so short-staffed at the clinic. Two of the other phlebotomists called out sick, which I don't even believe because one of them posted a picture on Instagram at the beach. And of course, it was a Tuesday, which is always our busiest day for fasting labs. People come in so cranky when they haven't had their coffee. This one guy actually yelled at me because I couldn't find his vein on the first try, but he was so dehydrated his veins were practically flat. I bought one of those giant water bottles with the motivational quotes on the side, like \"Keep Going!\" and \"Almost There!\" at the different time markers. It's really heavy to carry around when it's full, though. I accidentally dropped it in the breakroom last week and it bounced and cracked the plastic bottom. Water went everywhere. It took me twenty minutes to mop it up with those flimsy brown paper towels we have in the dispenser. They don't absorb anything, they just kind of push the water around. \n\nBut yeah, no, my mood is fine. It doesn't change what I know about the lab results.\n\nDoctor: Do you think the lab results were changed because of an ordinary mistake or mix-up, or because of something much more unusual or impossible?\n\nPatient: No, it’s definitely not an ordinary mistake. I mean, I’m here because for the past year I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system is deliberately changing or holding back parts of my dad’s lab results. It’s not just a typo. \n\nSpeaking of the clinic system, though, IT just updated our charting software last weekend and it’s a total disaster. It’s supposed to be this new fancy cloud-based thing, but it completely disconnected all the label printers in the draw stations. I spent half of Monday morning just trying to get a single barcode to print. It’s exactly like when I tried to set up my wireless printer at home. I bought this little HP printer on sale because I like to print out recipes instead of looking at my phone in the kitchen. I found this amazing recipe for a lemon blueberry loaf on Pinterest, but you know how those websites have like twenty pop-up ads and a whole ten-page story about the blogger's trip to Tuscany before you even get to the ingredients? I hate that. I just want to know how much baking powder to use! I ended up guessing on the lemon zest because the page kept freezing, and the bread came out super bitter. My dad wouldn't even eat it. \n\nBut anyway, with his labs... no matter how many doctors or family members tell me the numbers are fine, I know what I saw. I know the chart doesn’t match what I originally saw. And it’s just wearing me down, honestly. Fighting everyone on this for a year is exhausting.\n\nDoctor: Have you been able to keep your job and your usual responsibilities over this past year?\n\nPatient: Yeah, I mean, outside of the dispute about my dad’s records, I still keep my phlebotomy shifts, pay my bills, take care of myself, and manage my normal day-to-day responsibilities. I haven't missed any work over it, except for that one time my car wouldn't start. \n\nThat was a whole nightmare. It was a Tuesday, and I went out to start my Honda—it's a 2012 Civic, usually super reliable. I've had it since I took those couple semesters of college before I decided to just do the phlebotomy certification. Anyway, I turn the key and it just clicks. Click, click, click. I knew right away it was the battery. I had to call my neighbor, Mrs. Gable—the one with the Pomeranian—to see if she had jumper cables. She didn't, but she offered to drive me to AutoZone. Have you ever been in a car with someone who drives exactly five miles under the speed limit the entire time? It was agonizing. And her car smelled strongly of lavender air freshener, like, aggressively lavender. It gave me such a headache. We finally got the battery, but then the guy at the store wouldn't put it in for me because he said the terminals were too corroded. I had to watch a YouTube video on my phone right there in the parking lot to figure out how to clean them with baking soda and a toothbrush. I ruined my good scrub top doing it. \n\nBut yeah, I still go to work and do everything I need to do. Everything else is totally normal.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever believed that your thoughts were being controlled or inserted by someone else?\n\nPatient: No, I mean, my thoughts are just my own. I don't even know how someone would do that. Sometimes I feel like I have *too* many thoughts, though, you know? Like my brain just won't shut off at night. I actually tried downloading one of those meditation apps because my sister said it would help clear my head. \n\nBut the guy's voice on the guided sleep thing was so annoying. It sounded exactly like the automated voice when you call the cable company. Have you ever tried to get a real human on the phone with Comcast? I spent forty-five minutes on hold last week just trying to figure out why my bill went up twelve dollars. And the hold music is this terrible smooth jazz loop that cuts off right in the middle of a saxophone solo and starts over. It drove me insane. When I finally got a guy on the line, he said my 'promotional period' ended, which is such a scam because I never even signed up for a promotion. I just wanted the basic internet so I could stream Netflix. \n\nI've been rewatching Grey's Anatomy lately, even though it makes me yell at the TV. The way they draw blood on that show is so fake. They just jab the needle in without even anchoring the vein properly, and half the time the tourniquet isn't even tight. If I did that at the clinic, I'd have patients bruising all over their arms. They don't even use the right order of draw for the tubes! It just really bothers me when shows don't do their research. \n\nBut anyway, yeah, nobody is putting thoughts in my head or controlling them. It's just my own brain in there."
